summary: Hung Tran, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council GeoEconomics Center, argues in a January 2023 Econographics piece that record Fed reverse repo volume is an unhealthy development. Usage of the Fed's overnight reverse repo facility (ON RRP) reached $2.55 trillion at end-2022, driven by regulatory changes and money market funds' lack of alternatives. The author warns this draws activity away from private markets, undermines private benchmark rates such as SOFR and the Fed funds rate, and reduces Treasury revenue from the Fed.
one_line: Hung Tran argues that record Fed overnight reverse repo volume at end-2022 signals an unhealthy shift of short-term funding away from private markets.
key_facts: At the end of 2022, daily overnight reverse repo volume between the Fed and money market participants reached a new record high of $2.55 trillion.
The ON RRP facility consistently reached above $2 trillion since June 2022.
The Fed's reverse repo facility paid 4.3 percent to eligible participants at the time of the article, and interest on bank reserves was 4.4 percent.
The effective Fed funds rate was around 4.33 percent, within the targeted range of 4.25 percent to 4.5 percent.
The supplementary liquidity ratio (SLR) was relaxed in 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic and was restored in March 2021.
Money market funds' assets under management grew from around $3 trillion in 2012-2019 to around $5 trillion since early 2020.
The outstanding amount of US Treasury bills declined by $1.5 trillion as the United States extended the maturity of its borrowing.
ON RRPs account for more than 63 percent of the portfolios of money market funds.
The Fed has transferred about $1 trillion to the Treasury cumulatively since 2010, with a record annual payment of $109 billion in 2021.
The Fed is estimated to post a loss of $80 billion by the end of 2022 as it pays interest on ON RRP and bank reserves while reducing its holdings through QT.
Around $1 trillion in all private repo markets was used to calculate SOFR, which replaced Libor, at the end of 2022.
Around $100 billion in the interbank Fed funds market was traded at the end of 2022.
The author argues the Fed has become a 'money market maker of first resort' rather than a traditional 'lender of last resort' during financial crises.
The article was published on January 9, 2023 in the Atlantic Council's Econographics series.
